prompt: how do large language models like ChatGPT work

plan.title: How ChatGPT-style language models really work
plan.description: Large language models like ChatGPT predict the next word, over and over. This explainer covers tokens, training on text, attention, and why the answers can sound right yet be wrong.

beats.narration: ChatGPT does not look up answers. It does one simple thing, again and again: it guesses the next word. That single trick writes essays, code, and poems.

props.text: It just guesses the next word, again and again.

beats.narration: Think of your phone's autocomplete. Type "see you" and it suggests "soon". A large language model is that idea, grown enormously and trained on a huge amount of text.
First, text is chopped into small pieces called tokens. A token can be a whole word or just part of one. The model never sees letters the way we do.

props.definition: A small piece of text, a word or part of a word, that the model reads and writes.

beats.narration: Next comes training. The model reads vast amounts of text and plays a game: hide the next token, guess it, check the answer, and adjust. Billions of tiny dials get nudged each time.
After enough rounds, the model picks up grammar, facts, and styles of writing. Nobody typed in those rules. They emerged from patterns in the text.

props.alt: rows of books in a library

beats.narration: A key ingredient is attention. When the model reads a sentence, each word looks back at the other words to decide which ones matter. In "the dog chased its tail", "its" points back to the dog, and "tail" belongs to it.
When you ask a question, the model reads your words and scores every possible next token. It picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats until the answer is complete.
A little randomness is added to that choice, so the same question can get different answers. More randomness feels creative. Less feels steady and predictable.

props.heading: Randomness in the pick
items: Some chance, not always the top pick

beats.narration: Here is the catch. The model is built to sound likely, not to be certain. So it can state something false with total confidence. Check anything that matters.
So a language model is a next-word guesser, trained on oceans of text. Remember that, and you will know when to trust it and when to double-check.

props.text: A very well-read guesser: useful, but worth double-checking.
